learningObjective: Diagnose the accuracy trade-off of KV cache INT8 quantization in long-context LLM decoding.

canonicalClaims.claim: KV cache quantization introduces per-element error that softmax attention amplifies over long contexts; observed accuracy drops are typically small (~0.5% or less) at 32K context and can be traded for larger batch capacity or longer context.
conditions: The attention softmax normalizes over all context positions.
The KV quantization scheme (per-token, per-head) is reasonable — extremely coarse scales would produce larger drops.
nonImplications: Does not imply INT8 KV is safe for every workload; retrieval-heavy or long-form reasoning may see larger drops.
Does not imply FP8 KV is always better than INT8 KV; depends on distribution.

misconceptions.claim: INT8 KV cache quantization is bit-exact with FP16 KV cache.
misconceptions.whyWrong: INT8 loses precision; even with per-token scaling, the quantized KV differs from the FP16 KV element-wise.

misconceptions.claim: The accuracy drop at long context is due to INT8's range being insufficient for long-context activations.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Per-token/per-head scaling handles the range issue; the drop comes from softmax's cumulative sensitivity to logit noise across many positions.

misconceptions.claim: KV cache quantization does not free GPU memory because the allocator still reserves FP16 slots.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Paged attention allocators respect the actual quantized element size; memory savings are real.

misconceptions.claim: Using UINT8 instead of INT8 for KV quantization eliminates the accuracy drop.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Signed vs unsigned changes the value range mapping (via zero-point), not the quantization noise floor per element.

implementationFacts: TensorRT-LLM supports INT8 KV with per-token / per-head scaling.
vLLM 0.4+ supports INT8 and FP8 KV cache modes.
FP8 KV is often preferred over INT8 on Hopper due to native FP8 attention support.
performanceScenarios: Doubling batch capacity from 2 to 4 for a memory-constrained server can raise throughput by ~1.8× (batching amortization is not linear).
